{"slug": "what-is-an-api-plain-english-guide", "title": "What Is an API? A Plain-English Guide (2026)", "metaTitle": "What Is an API? A Plain-English Guide (2026)", "metaDescription": "A clear, jargon-free explanation of what an API is, how it works, and why it matters when building software \u2014 with real examples anyone can follow.", "targetKeyword": "what is an api (plain-english guide)", "category": "Glossary", "bodyHtml": "

The short definition

An API, short for Application Programming Interface, is a defined way for one piece of software to ask another piece of software for something \u2014 data or an action \u2014 without needing to know how that other system works internally. You send a request in a format the other system understands, and you get a response back. That's the whole idea. Everything else is detail.

The word interface is the key part. An API is a boundary. It hides the messy internals of a system and exposes a small, predictable set of things you're allowed to ask for. You don't need to know how a system stores its data, what language it's written in, or how its servers are organized. You just need to know the rules for asking.

The restaurant analogy

Picture a restaurant. You sit down with a menu, which lists exactly what you're allowed to order. You don't walk into the kitchen and cook the meal yourself, and you don't need to know how the stove works, where the ingredients came from, or how many cooks are back there. You tell the waiter what you want from the menu, the waiter carries that request to the kitchen, and the kitchen sends a finished plate back out.

The menu is the API. It defines exactly what requests are valid. The waiter is the messenger who carries your request to the kitchen and brings the response back. The kitchen is the system doing the actual work, completely hidden from you. If the restaurant changes its kitchen equipment or swaps out a supplier, you never notice, because the menu \u2014 the interface \u2014 stayed the same. That's exactly how a good API behaves: the internals can change freely as long as the interface stays stable.

A real example: a weather app

Say you open a weather app and it shows today's forecast for your city. The app itself doesn't own any weather data. It doesn't have sensors, satellites, or meteorologists. Instead, it sends a request to a weather service's API, something like a request for the current forecast for a specific location. The weather service's servers process that request and send back a response, usually a structured chunk of data with the temperature, conditions, and forecast for the next few days.

The app then takes that raw data and displays it as a clean screen with icons and numbers. The API is the plumbing in between: a defined, reliable way for the app to ask the weather service for information and get a predictable answer back, every time, without the app's developers ever needing to know how the weather service actually forecasts weather.

Why this matters when you're building software

APIs are the reason modern software doesn't get built from scratch every time. Instead of every company running its own weather satellites, payment processing network, or mapping system, they call an API built by someone who already solved that problem. This is also why software teams can work in parallel: as long as everyone agrees on the interface, the frontend team and the backend team can build their pieces independently, and either side can be rewritten later without breaking the other, as long as the API contract stays the same.

It's also why bugs and outages often trace back to an API changing unexpectedly, or a request being sent in the wrong format. Understanding APIs is really understanding how independent pieces of software agree to talk to each other.

Where Kodely fits today

It's worth being precise here. Kodely is an AI website builder: you describe a site in plain English, and it generates a real Vite and React application with actual component files you can preview live and publish to a public URL. A Kodely-generated frontend can absolutely display data, including data that would normally come from an API, in its layout and design.

What Kodely doesn't do today is wire up a live third-party API for you. There's no built-in way to connect something like a payment processor or a mapping service into a generated site yet. If you're building a project to learn how APIs work in practice, Kodely is a fast way to get the visual, front-end half of that project running in minutes, with the connected-data half still to come.

Related terms

  • Frontend: the part of an application the user sees and interacts with directly \u2014 the layout, buttons, and screens rendered in a browser.
  • Backend: the server-side part of an application that handles logic, stores data, and typically exposes the APIs that a frontend calls.
  • Webhook: almost the reverse of a typical API call. Instead of your app asking a service for data, a webhook is a way for a service to automatically send your app a message the moment something happens, like a payment going through.

FAQ

Is an API the same thing as a website?

No. A website is built for humans to read in a browser. An API is built for software to talk to other software, usually exchanging structured data rather than a visual page.

Do I need to know how to code to use an API?

To call an API directly and handle its response, yes, you generally need some programming knowledge. But you interact with the results of APIs constantly without writing code, every time an app on your phone shows you live data.

What does REST API mean?

REST is one common style, or set of conventions, for designing APIs, especially ones used over the web. It's a way of organizing requests and responses consistently, not a different concept from the API idea itself.

Can I add a real API to a site I build with Kodely?

Not today. Kodely generates real frontend code you can view and publish, but connecting a live third-party API isn't a built-in feature yet. Kodely is a genuinely useful way to spin up the visual side of a project fast, honestly scoped to what it does right now.

Want to see how quickly Kodely turns a plain-English description into a real, working site? See it in action \u2014 build free.
